2026-06963.headline: Stablecoin freeze power: a FinCEN/OFAC proposal would require issuers to be able to block, freeze and reject transactions
2026-06963.what_changed: A joint proposed rule (91 FR 18582; RIN 1506-AB73; docket FINCEN-2026-0100) would treat permitted payment stablecoin issuers (PPSIs) as financial institutions under the Bank Secrecy Act and require AML and sanctions-compliance programs. Comments closed in June 2026, and no final rule was found.
2026-06963.summary: Under the GENIUS Act (P.L. 119-27), an issuer may issue payment stablecoins only if it can technically comply with lawful orders to seize, freeze, burn or block its coins. This joint FinCEN/OFAC proposal would make that part of ongoing compliance programs: customer identification, suspicious-activity and currency-transaction reporting, sanctions screening, and the ability to block or freeze. Comments closed June 9, and there's no final rule yet. Some industry write-ups said freezes would reach tokens traded between holders, but the Act exempts direct person-to-person and self-custody transfers, so that claim isn't supported. Coin Center separately objected (Aug 21) to applying customer-ID rules to secondary-market transactions. Separately, on Nov 2 Tether, which issues the USDT stablecoin, said it froze more than $1.5 billion in USDT within 30 minutes of an Oct 29 exchange hack that it said the FBI tied to North Korea. That was the company's own anti-theft step, not a government order, but it shows how fast an issuer can freeze coins.
2026-06963.why_it_matters: Freeze and seize capability built into the token itself becomes a legal condition of issuing the main regulated digital-dollar instrument. That gives authorities a built-in way to stop specific holders' funds on a court or agency order.
2026-06963.why_it_might_not: Freezes require a lawful order tied to specific coins or accounts, comparable to existing bank freezes under sanctions and court process, and major issuers already freeze voluntarily.

2026-21786.headline: Treasury proposes rules for the outbound investment law (COINS Act): a wider list of countries and technologies, with some deals banned and others requiring notice
2026-21786.org: U.S. Treasury, Office of Investment Security
2026-21786.what_changed: Treasury published a proposed rule (91 FR 67396; RIN 1505-AC94; docket TREAS-DO-2026-0595) to implement the COINS Act, which Congress passed in the FY2026 NDAA on Dec 18, 2025. It would create a new 31 CFR Part 851 to replace the Part 850 program that has applied since Jan 2, 2025.
2026-21786.summary: U.S. persons (citizens, green-card holders, U.S. entities and their foreign branches) would have to notify Treasury of some investments, and would be barred from others, in 'covered foreign persons' tied to countries of concern that work in listed technologies. Covered deals include buying equity or contingent equity, certain convertible or equity-like loans, joint ventures, greenfield projects, directing a foreign person's deal, and some limited-partner stakes in non-U.S. funds. U.S. parents would also answer for deals made by foreign subsidiaries they control. The countries of concern grow from China (including Hong Kong and Macau) to also cover Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia and Venezuela 'under the regime of Nicolas Maduro', which Treasury says no longer exists. The technologies grow from semiconductors, quantum and AI (renamed 'super intelligence systems') to add high-performance computing/supercomputing and hypersonics; Treasury's press release also lists biotechnology. The statute exempts bank lending, payment processing and clearing, underwriting, prime brokerage and global custody, plus de minimis deals at amounts Treasury has not yet set. National-interest exemptions are available.
2026-21786.why_it_matters: This is the only live federal framework that requires advance notice for, or outright bans, Americans' investments abroad. It now rests on a statute instead of an executive order, so it is more durable. The proposal widens the countries and sectors covered and lets Treasury add more technology categories through notice and comment. It also reaches indirect routes (fund-of-funds and LP stakes, structures that hide a U.S. person's role) and makes 'reasonable and diligent inquiry' a compliance duty.
2026-21786.why_it_might_not: It is targeted at national security. It covers only specified technology activities by entities linked to six named countries, and it does not limit ordinary payments, bank lending, custody or deposits. Treasury reports only about 100 notifications in roughly 21 months of the existing program. For most Americans it limits nothing about moving or holding money.

fdic-2026-22495.headline: FDIC proposal would move the largest banks under the 2008 'provisional hold' rule, for use if they fail

Holds apply only after a failure, while the FDIC separates insured from uninsured money. Some pass-through account holders, such as deposit brokers and agents, would have to be told they might not reach those deposits after a failure until they give the FDIC the required data.

genius-implementation-2026.what_changed: The OCC adopted its final GENIUS rule (new 12 CFR Part 15) on Oct 21, 2026, effective Jan 18, 2027. The Fed proposed reserve, capital and application rules on Sept 24, 2026, with comments due Nov 30. Treasury's section 3 proposal (2026-16796) closed for comment on Oct 19, 2026.
genius-implementation-2026.summary: From Jan 18, 2027, only licensed issuers may issue payment stablecoins in the U.S. Issuers must back coins fully with reserves such as short-term Treasury bills and meet redemption, capital and risk standards. Starting July 18, 2028, digital-asset service providers may not offer U.S. persons stablecoins from issuers that are not permitted. The OCC set BSA, AML and sanctions requirements aside for a separate rulemaking with Treasury. Treasury's proposal defines 'issue' to exclude transfers 'required by a lawful order'.
genius-implementation-2026.why_it_matters: This is building a regulated private digital-dollar system in which every compliant token carries freeze capability. It requires reserves in short-term Treasuries, which creates captive demand for government debt but only within the issuer sector.
genius-implementation-2026.why_it_might_not: It is licensing and prudential regulation of issuers. Holders face no new limits on withdrawing, redeeming or moving funds, and the rules include redemption standards.

hr1799-119.headline: House bill to raise cash and suspicious-activity reporting thresholds awaits a floor vote
hr1799-119.org: Rep. Loudermilk (sponsor); House Financial Services Committee
hr1799-119.what_changed: H.R. 1799, the Financial Reporting Threshold Modernization Act, was reported with an amendment on Mar 19, 2026 (H. Rept. 119-556; Union Calendar No. 478). No later floor action was confirmed.
hr1799-119.summary: As reported, the bill would raise the $10,000 cash-reporting threshold for non-financial businesses (31 U.S.C. 5331) to $30,000. It would also raise SAR thresholds from $5,000 to $10,000 and from $2,000 to $3,000, raise MSB-definition thresholds from $1,000 to $3,000, and index all of them to inflation every 5 years. It also directs a Treasury review of CTR and SAR requirements. This researcher did not verify the exact change to the bank CTR threshold under 31 U.S.C. 5313 in the reported text. A June 2026 House hearing, including Cato Institute testimony, also pushed to raise or repeal Bank Secrecy Act reporting thresholds.
hr1799-119.why_it_matters: It would roll back cash surveillance that has grown in real terms because the thresholds were never indexed. It also cuts against the GTO trend of lowering thresholds.
hr1799-119.why_it_might_not: It has not passed the House and has no Senate action, and it expires on Jan 3, 2027.

crypto-exchange-withdrawal-pauses-2026-1.headline: Hacks, hacking threats and outside-vendor failures lead crypto platforms outside the U.S. to pause withdrawals; South Korea's Gopax is still halted, and Brazil's Nubank paused for part of a day
crypto-exchange-withdrawal-pauses-2026-1.org: Binance; Gopax (South Korea); Mercado Bitcoin, Nubank and Mercado Pago (Brazil)
crypto-exchange-withdrawal-pauses-2026-1.who: Private cryptocurrency exchanges and fintech apps
crypto-exchange-withdrawal-pauses-2026-1.what_changed: On Nov 6, Brazil's Nubank halted crypto deposits and withdrawals, and Mercado Pago blocked some crypto transfers to outside wallets, after problems at outside providers; Mercado Pago tied its problem to an incident at a risk-monitoring and anti-money-laundering vendor. Nubank restored deposits and withdrawals at 10 p.m. that night; Mercado Pago hadn't said by Nov 7 whether its transfers had resumed. South Korea's Gopax, which halted withdrawals, trading and deposits on Nov 6 after hacking threats, still had no date to reopen on Nov 8 and was handling withdrawals only by manual review; a senior Korean financial regulator said Gopax is believed to have received about two threatening emails and appears to have reported to authorities before suspending service, and the Financial Supervisory Service plans to meet exchange and custody firms' security chiefs on Nov 19. Binance, hacked for about $6.3 billion on Oct 29, has kept reopening withdrawals in phases since Nov 1, and Brazil's Mercado Bitcoin halted withdrawals Nov 2 after about $40 million was drained.
crypto-exchange-withdrawal-pauses-2026-1.summary: These were company decisions after thefts, threats or vendor failures, not government limits on customers' money. Binance said it would cover losses, and Binance is Gopax's majority shareholder. Stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle froze wallets holding stolen coins, about $3 billion in total, which shows the freeze ability that U.S. rules will require issuers to have for lawful orders. The Brazil pauses show that a failure at an outside data or compliance vendor can stop transfers even when the platform itself isn't hacked. Binance.US, a separate U.S. platform, said it was not affected by the hack.
crypto-exchange-withdrawal-pauses-2026-1.why_it_matters: Withdrawal pauses at big platforms can spread fear and claims that capital controls are starting. The stablecoin freezes show how quickly issuers can block coins, an ability U.S. rules will soon require, and the Brazil cases show how one outside compliance vendor can halt transfers at several firms.
crypto-exchange-withdrawal-pauses-2026-1.why_it_might_not: The pauses were company security or technical steps at platforms outside the U.S., not government orders to limit customers' money; Nubank reopened the same night and Binance has been reopening in phases.

2026-22809.headline: FinCEN and the Fed drop a 2020 plan to cut the record-keeping threshold for transfers abroad from $3,000 to $250
2026-22809.org: FinCEN (Treasury) and the Federal Reserve Board
2026-22809.what_changed: FinCEN and the Fed announced on Nov 6, 2026, that they were withdrawing their October 2020 joint proposal (85 FR 68005; RIN 1506-AB41). The withdrawal notice (FR Doc 2026-22809) was published in the Federal Register on Nov 9, making the withdrawal official.
2026-22809.summary: The 2020 proposal would have lowered, from $3,000 to $250, the amount at which banks and money transmitters must collect and keep sender and recipient details on funds transfers that begin or end outside the U.S., and the amount at which FinCEN's travel rule requires passing those details along the payment chain. It also would have stated that these rules cover crypto and digital assets with legal-tender status. The agencies said they received nearly 3,000 comments, mostly opposed; that more than five years had passed; and that crypto markets and laws, including the GENIUS Act, have changed. They said no similar final rule will be issued without a new chance for public comment. The $3,000 threshold stays in place.
2026-22809.why_it_matters: It retires a long-pending plan that would have brought far more everyday transfers abroad, such as family remittances, under record-keeping and pass-along requirements, and the agencies committed to new public comment before trying anything similar.
2026-22809.why_it_might_not: The existing $3,000 rules stay in place, and the agencies left room for future changes aimed at crypto. Tighter reporting can still come through other tools, such as geographic targeting orders like the Minnesota and Southwest border orders, or rules to carry out FATF's new payment-transparency standard.

It doesn't change existing reporting or sanctions duties and has no end date. MEXC said its operations were normal and that it had started an independent review of its anti-money-laundering and sanctions controls. The order names one foreign company; it doesn't limit transfers to other platforms or ordinary transfers abroad.

intl-imf-stablecoin-flows-capital-contro.what_changed: An Oct 1, 2026 IMF working paper (No. 2026/211) estimated stablecoin flows for 188 countries, and an Oct 8 departmental paper (No. 2026/021) set out initial policy considerations for foreign-currency stablecoins. Both came out before the first report; added Nov 7 for context, not as new movement.
intl-imf-stablecoin-flows-capital-contro.summary: The working paper estimates $21.4 trillion in gross international stablecoin flows from 2018 to 2025, with emerging and developing economies holding three quarters of stablecoins. It finds stablecoin activity rises about 30% in the six months after a country restricts capital outflows and doesn't fall back when the restrictions end, and that holdings rise about 75% within a year of a currency crisis. The departmental paper says stablecoins issued mostly in U.S. dollars by a few jurisdictions could reshape capital flows and currency substitution in other countries, and it outlines possible responses on macro-financial policy, regulation, data collection and international cooperation. These are staff views, not official IMF policy.
intl-imf-stablecoin-flows-capital-contro.official_acknowledgment: IMF staff research with standard disclaimers
intl-imf-stablecoin-flows-capital-contro.us_link: Most stablecoins are U.S.-dollar coins issued by a few firms, so other countries' responses could affect how dollar stablecoins move across borders. The papers concern other countries' policies, not limits on Americans.
intl-imf-stablecoin-flows-capital-contro.why_it_matters: It documents people turning to stablecoins when their countries restrict money leaving, which could push governments to aim future capital controls at stablecoin flows.
intl-imf-stablecoin-flows-capital-contro.why_it_might_not: It's research and early policy thinking about other countries, not a recommendation to limit Americans, and the U.S. already regulates its own dollar stablecoins under the GENIUS Act.

dol-1210-AC38-401k-alternatives.summary: The March 31, 2026 proposal would give employers and other plan managers a legal safe harbor when they add funds holding alternative assets to 401(k) menus, if they weigh six factors: performance, fees, liquidity, valuation, benchmarks and complexity. Alternative assets include private equity and debt, real estate, commodities, infrastructure, lifetime-income strategies and actively managed funds that hold digital assets. The rule carries out an August 2025 executive order (EO 14330). It wouldn't require any plan to offer these funds; it deals with how plan managers choose investments and doesn't address withdrawals or rollovers. The proposal notes such assets can carry higher fees and be harder to sell and to price.

dol-1210-AC38-401k-alternatives.why_it_might_not: It's a legal safe harbor, not a mandate: employers still decide what their plans offer, the final text could change, and the proposal doesn't address withdrawals or rollovers. foster-real-time-regulatory-study-act-dr.what_changed: On Nov 5, 2026, Rep. Foster released a discussion draft of the Real-Time Regulatory Study Act. It would direct the Federal Reserve Board, working with other financial regulators, to develop, test and publicly release open-source demonstration software that could streamline banks' reporting and give regulators real-time information on the condition of financial institutions.
foster-real-time-regulatory-study-act-dr.summary: A one-page summary lists modules such as regulatory dashboards, automated bank and credit union reports, stress tests on historical and current data, AI risk monitoring, and automated fraud and anti-money-laundering screening. The draft calls for an interim report to Congress within 180 days, a systemwide test within 18 months and a final assessment within two years. According to the summary, no live customer accounts would be used and no actions would be taken based on test results. Foster's release says AI and round-the-clock payment systems could spread financial stress quickly, and that real-time tools could help regulators respond faster and prepare for orderly bank resolutions. It is a draft, not an introduced bill.
foster-real-time-regulatory-study-act-dr.why_it_matters: Real-time data would give regulators a faster view of trouble at banks, such as sudden deposit outflows, and shape how quickly they could respond to a run. Its author is likely to gain influence when his party takes control of Congress.

intl-asia-market-support-2026-11-06.what_changed: On Nov 9, the steps announced Nov 6 took effect: Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission cut intraday short sales of borrowed shares to 3% of a stock's average daily volume over the prior 30 trading days (from 30%) and raised the minimum short-sale margin from 90% to 130%, and South Korea exempted brokerages from the 140% minimum collateral ratio on margin loans through Jan 31. The steps aim to support prices: buying stocks, curbing bets on falling prices, and easing margin calls so fewer investors are forced to sell. Several people told Reuters that Taiwan's Finance Ministry asked state-owned banks to support the market. Taiwan's fund cited record foreign selling of NT$994 billion in October and NT$524 billion more in November through Nov 6. None of these steps limits bank withdrawals, currency exchange or moving money abroad.
intl-asia-market-support-2026-11-06.why_it_matters: It shows how quickly governments step into markets during a sharp selloff, including limits on one kind of trade. Steps like these can fuel claims that broader limits on selling or moving money are next.
intl-asia-market-support-2026-11-06.why_it_might_not: State stock-buying funds and short-sale curbs are familiar, temporary tools in Asian markets. They don't stop investors from selling shares they own or from moving their money, and the U.S. has no similar state stock fund.

Some outlets called it a banking crisis, but it was a technical failure lasting about six hours, not a government action or a bank run. It has no link to U.S. banks.

paraguay-ueno-bank-resolution-2026-11.headline: Paraguay's central bank takes over failed digital lender Ueno Bank; accounts are frozen while a state fund repays savers in stages
paraguay-ueno-bank-resolution-2026-11.org: Banco Central del Paraguay (Paraguay's central bank) and its banking and securities supervisors
paraguay-ueno-bank-resolution-2026-11.what_changed: On Nov 2, 2026, Paraguay's central bank voted unanimously to put Ueno Bank into resolution (a state-run wind-down) after the bank's solvency ratio fell below half the legal minimum. Ueno's services stopped early on Nov 3, locking customers out of their accounts except for payouts from the state Deposit Guarantee Fund, which began the night of Nov 5. By Nov 8, 64% of Ueno's 1,867,531 depositor accounts, almost 1.2 million, had been paid a total of Gs 994.6 billion (about $158 million), and the central bank said it would start paying depositors who also owe Ueno money on Nov 9, after subtracting their overdue debts. On Nov 6, Paraguay's Senate removed President Santiago Peña from office over his links to the bank.
paraguay-ueno-bank-resolution-2026-11.summary: Ueno launched as a fintech in 2021 and began operating as a bank in November 2023; it says it had 2.9 million customers, around 60% of Paraguay's adults. The guarantee fund covers up to 75 monthly minimum wages per depositor (Gs 228.3 million, about $38,000). The first payments, an advance of up to 40 minimum wages (Gs 121.76 million), went to depositors with no debts at Ueno and an account at another bank; savings certificates and larger balances have no payment date yet. Paraguay's securities regulator, part of the central bank, briefly suspended withdrawals from some mutual funds that held Ueno investments while their value was checked, and began lifting those pauses on Nov 4 and 5. The central bank says the problem is particular to Ueno: other banks' ATMs, branches and online banking kept working, though some banking apps slowed as people rushed to open new accounts, and it called social-media rumors of takeovers at other institutions false. Prosecutors are investigating the collapse, and Paraguay's state pension fund had about $355 million at Ueno.
paraguay-ueno-bank-resolution-2026-11.why_it_matters: It shows in real time what a large bank failure means for savers: accounts frozen, insured money returned in stages over several days, and a regulator briefly pausing withdrawals from investment funds tied to the bank. That is the kind of situation U.S. failed-bank rules, such as the FDIC's pending 'provisional hold' proposal for the largest banks, are designed to handle.
paraguay-ueno-bank-resolution-2026-11.why_it_might_not: It is one failed bank in another country, handled under Paraguay's own deposit-guarantee law, and the fund pauses lasted only days. In the U.S., deposits are insured to at least $250,000 at each FDIC-insured bank, and the FDIC's list shows no U.S. bank failures since Sept 25.

next_milestone.what: Payouts to the remaining depositor groups, including savings certificates and larger balances (no dates set); Paraguay's state pension fund pays the 32,000 pensioners who banked at Ueno through other banks on Nov 17
